title: How Backrooms Built Its Liminal World With 30,000 Square Feet of Sets
excerpt: Backrooms combined practical construction with a visual effects workflow informed by Kane Parsons’ Blender experience. The production used more than 30,000 square feet of sets across four sound stages.
seo_title: Backrooms: Inside Its Practical Sets and Visual Effects
seo_description: Danny Vermette and Ed Douglas explain how Backrooms combined practical construction, Blender and four sound stages to create its unsettling liminal spaces.
body_md:
Before Kane Parsons' Backrooms became a film with a reported $400 million worldwide box office total, its fictional universe had developed through a popular YouTube series. In a Variety report published on November 25, 2026, production designer Danny Vermette and visual effects supervisor Ed Douglas discussed how they expanded that internet-born world for a feature film.

## Bringing the original workflow into cinema

The original online series comprised 22 episodes, ranging in length from two to 45 minutes. Neither Vermette nor Douglas was familiar with the material before being approached about the film. Both began exploring the existing videos to understand the visual language that Parsons had established.

Douglas learned that the director had used Blender to create the original environments. Rather than completely replacing that process with a conventional feature-film visual effects workflow, the filmmakers developed an approach that incorporated elements of both.

Set in 1991, the film follows Clark, played by Chiwetel Ejiofor, a furniture store owner who discovers a passage into an unfamiliar world of seemingly endless spaces. Carpeting, yellow wallpaper and ordinary architectural details help define its distinctive atmosphere.

## Building the spaces actors actually touch

The production prioritized constructing the environments with which performers would directly interact. Vermette had to work within financial and physical space constraints while providing enough practical material for the visual effects team to extend the architecture digitally.

Physical walls, ceilings and lighting gave the artists references for maintaining consistency between photographed environments and computer-generated extensions. The furniture store basement and the first Backrooms environment were built beside each other, allowing performers and camera operators to move between them.

Creating the illusion of passing through walls required a separate visual effects process. Blue screens allowed the walls to be reconstructed digitally during post-production. Douglas explained that the resulting images required meticulous attention to the interaction of shadows and surfaces. The filmmakers avoided conventional fantasy effects that might make the transitions look overtly magical.

Vertical environments presented another challenge. The team built the portions performers needed to touch and traverse, while digital work expanded the surrounding architecture beyond the physical construction.

In total, Backrooms used more than 30,000 square feet of sets and four sound stages. That scale illustrates how the production combined tangible environments with digital extensions instead of relying exclusively on either method. The practical construction became the foundation for preserving the recognizable appearance of Parsons' original universe.
